pitch_detail.notes: Crack and face climbing through bulges and overlaps on orange flakes and knobs, on a face that is slightly overhanging and tiring on the forearms for a while. A small narrow-headed cam, roughly alien size, is useful soon after the start, and protection improves after the first 30 ft or so. Angle gradually rightward through crack systems into pale rock along the face's right margin, beneath a band of roofs. A hand crack slanting left cuts through them; above it, cracks across gentle ground lead to a belay under a shattered, crumbly yellowish headwall. Bring a #6 cam and small or offset cams for that belay.
Finish however you like: merge left with the neighbouring route, go right toward the other neighbour, or tackle the headwall directly to reach the summit ridge.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with lengths from feet; no per-pitch grade is given (5.7 is for the whole route).

pitch_detail.notes: Use face holds to climb the shallow light-coloured gully, then leave it rightward by a tidy crack onto orange rock. A brief, steeper stretch of dependable face moves is the crux and slips past the right end of the large roof. Belay on gear where the slope eases. Long slings suit the chicken-head holds.
One brief steep, well-featured bit, after which gentler and fun scrambling carries on along the remaining ridge to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with the grades given. No lengths stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb featured rock up and right toward a 20 ft overhanging crack set in an obtuse corner. The crack is the crux and is a struggle. The belay is on a large ledge system above it.
Start from the ledge's left end, using the cracks in the face above, and continue until the line merges with the neighbouring route.
Choose a line through the final steep section, then scramble easily to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches with lengths from feet; no pitch grades given (5.9 is the route grade, crux identified on P1).

pitch_detail.notes: Start by stepping right from the belay corner at the base of the neighbouring route onto flakes. The gently overhanging face offers flakes and knobs on orange stone. Go around the main roofs by their left side, then belay under a broken, crumbly headwall of pale yellow rock.
Finish however you prefer: join the neighbouring route, or take the headwall to the summit ridge.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with lengths from feet; no pitch grades given.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the big slot. If the slot itself is hard or awkward, the orange face on either side is a fine alternative. Step right onto the orange arete either immediately on entering or below the bush. Above the bush go up the crack-and-corner or the orange face to its right, with final corner moves to a stance on scalloped rock under grey double roofs.

Two options. Right option (about 60 ft): leave the belay by traversing out right at the roof's end, continue about 25 ft to a crack of finger to thin-hand size that curves back up and left, and belay on a roomy stance beneath the next roof. Direct option (about 40 ft): climb the roof itself using #4 and #5 cams, finishing at the same stance. Both belays take a #5 and #6 cam; other gear can be improvised.

Both options start by getting around the roof on good holds on its left. Right option (about 200 ft): go up and right on orange rock left of the slot to a big stance beneath a grey headwall on the slot's right side. Left option (about 100 ft): keep traversing left roughly 50 ft until the angle eases, then up to a roomy ledge below a stripe of high-quality orange rock.
From the right option, it is easy ground to the top. From the left option, climb the orange stripe, angle up and right at its top where the difficulty eases, and scamper to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote four entries; the text gives alternative lines on pitches 2 to 4, so their lengths appear as ranges in the notes rather than as single numbers. No grades given per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on twin cracks or a lieback flake that faces right, clip one bolt, and carry on up to the roof. Traverse right beneath the roof, which may need some cleaning of vegetation.
A short pitch: power out the burly hand-to-fist crack through the roof on the right, pull the lip onto easy hands, and reach a comfortable ledge. This roof is the hardest climbing on the route.

Step left to a vegetated hand crack and climb it to a high bolt, which can be clipped from the crack. Downclimb left to a slabby ledge and then go up easier ground to the anchor. Do not leave gear on the crack after clipping the bolt. Pitches 3 to 10 each run about 30 to 35 m and can often be linked.
An awkward groove on the left, then a shallow right-facing corner.
Shallow cracks and open face, with a handful of bolts for protection.
Steep jugs from the belay, clip a bolt, then hands through a small roof. At some point shift right to the next crack system.
Go up and right from the anchor, climbing a right-facing corner to a roof and hand crack.
Moderate climbing straight up a short slab to the anchor.
Move left from the anchor into an alcove, pull out of it, and continue straight up.

Face and finger climbing up from the belay, avoiding the dirtier ground on the left. Move left along a ledge toward a chimney with a table-sized flake wedged in it, pass this and a final stemming chimney, and belay at the anchor on the right.

review.changed: Wrote all ten pitches. Length given only for P1; the other pitches share a 30-35 m range stated in the P3 notes. No rappel table: the text gives a partial rappel description (second anchor to a pedestal, then the ground), not a full station list.

pitch_detail.notes: An obvious dark streak leads through one brief steep bit, then the slope lessens up to a ledge anchor that divides the face. This pitch is bolted.
Go up the corner to the right to the foot of a second black streak, then follow it for steady, moderate climbing to a natural belay beneath the White Flake itself. This pitch is bolted.
Climb the White Flake directly, curving left with it, and belay where the angle fades. Take gear to 4 inches.

rappel_detail.station: small tree beside the White Flake crack
rappel_detail.anchor: rap station several feet right of the tree
rappel_detail.notes: Follow the flake crack to a small tree; the station sits a few feet to its right. With two 60 m ropes, descend under the headwall, over one short vertical bit, to a second station that hides beneath the headwall and is hard to see until you are on it.
Descend vertically to the anchor that caps the neighbouring Jabberwalky route; it sits atop a small arch and is likewise easy to miss from a distance.

rappel_detail.station: anchor at the top of Jabberwalky
rappel_detail.notes: A short rap reaches the next station.
A 60 m rap down the neighbouring Aoxomoxoa line ends at the big sandy ledge. Recommended for children or anyone unsure of Tuolumne friction.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches and a four-rappel table taken from the stated rap descent; only the last rap has a stated length. Walk-off alternative not tabled.

pitch_detail.notes: Unprotected slab for a long way, or the corner on the left where hollow-sounding gear is available. The lead bolts that once protected the slab are gone. Belay in the corner on medium cams. A 70 m rope may be needed to reach another gear belay if running the corner as a single full pitch.

Climb the corner above; its crack pinches down at the top. Either exit right to a neighbouring route where the angle is lower, near the last decent piece, or move left onto the slab over the corner and run it out vertically, which takes a 70 m rope, to a flake that accepts a #3 or #4 cam.
Keep going to the tree standing under the headwall, which lets you set up the rappel from the ringed glue-in bolts there.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches as described; the stored count is 2. No lengths given. No rappel table: only a single rappel with two ropes from the headwall glue-ins is described.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 2 but the text describes three. The text says the lead bolts were removed; the stored row's protection may need review.

pitch_detail.notes: Cracks that trend rightward reach a wide level ledge, with a big sharp-edged dihedral rising from its right side. Dark knobs keep the climbing enjoyable and reasonable.

Climb the dihedral, step left over a block, and return right to the foot of a left-facing dihedral with a short but lovely finger-width splitter. Climb to the foot of a big flake projecting overhead, place a cam, and layback it: solid 5.9 moves, great exposure, wider gear during the layback and good pieces above and below. Above, trend back left up knobby face to a flat stance under a loose-looking gully.

Pass carefully through the gully on its left side, aiming for a golden tower with a shallow right-facing corner. Reach its base via cracks on the gully's left, climb the corner on good gear, and continue over blockier, broken terrain until rope drag forces a belay on sandy ledges below the summit. Fourth to fifth class scrambling finishes the route.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches with grades and metre lengths as given.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the left-facing corner to a good ledge. Some thin gear is needed.

Leaving the belay, work up and right on steeper features to escape the corner system, using one bolt. Cross a grubby ledge and a tight squeeze in brittle crystalline rock, then aim toward the large pine visible from the bivy and belay on gear above it. The linked section includes 5.7 climbing; splitting it would cut rope drag.
Trend right, then descend slightly into the wide chimney separating the pillar from the main wall. Blocky ground goes up to a ledge at the notch's top.

The obvious ramp climbs leftward across the south face. When protection ends, exit at a step in the feature onto the textured face on the left and belay at bolts, or keep linking: orange plates steepen along the dragon's-back with slung horns and one bolt to a small ledge, then a bulge above (#3 or #4 cam) to a bolted belay. Grades quoted are 5.9 for the first part and 5.10b for the second.
West-side face climbing on jugs with large huecos. Protected by gear, slings and one bolt. Ends in a snug corner with a bolted belay.

Get over the large boulder above the belay, then bridge across a gap and cross into face climbing that keeps getting easier up to the top. The linked section is 5.9 then 5.7; belaying after the gap would reduce rope drag.

review.changed: Wrote six entries, combining the linked pitches as the text does (2-3, 5-6, 8-9). Lengths from feet. No rappel table: the descent is described in general terms (rappel from the pseudo-summit into the notch and again from the true summit).
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 10; the text describes six entries covering up to nine pitch numbers.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a hand crack toward a pod and up to face moves above your gear, then shift right to a crack with good protection. The belay is the ledge under the stack of dark blocks.
Be careful on the huge detached block, continue up, and step right to reach ledges above. Rated PG.
Move up into the corner and climb it with face and layback moves for a long, very enjoyable pitch.

Continue up the corner with layback and face moves and a short chimney or offwidth. A lone bolt marks the spot to swing across into the right-hand cracks; the lichen-coated corner, around 5.11, is the alternative to the ledge.

Stem past the block guarding the chimney entrance and chimney up. When it feels desperate, exit left onto 5.4 terrain; if you cannot find protection you are on route. Rope drag is heavy up to the base of a splitter offwidth, and the loose detached blocks need care.
A clean offwidth that changes size and demands several techniques. Lichen is plentiful.
Starting in the ridge notch, go right up to the crest and follow it to the first top, which may be the true summit. Unrope and scramble at third to fourth class to the other summit.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P7 with lengths from feet. The initial scramble (pitch 0, 3rd class to about 5.5, soloable) is left out.
review.other_findings: Stored grade includes A0 and the text mentions no aid; top free grade in the text is 5.10c. Stored count 7 matches.

pitch_detail.notes: The red corner of pitch 2 is visible from the base. Scramble up blocks, then make a 5.9 stem to reach a belay stance. The belay is on gear.

Hand cracks lead to the foot of a right-facing red corner (hands and fists). Then hand-traverse 90 degrees left on jugs and climb a right-facing corner to a ledge. Leave this corner by a tough mantel, or avoid the mantel by bypassing it on the left; the mantel may be harder than the pitch grade but is well protected. Belay on a large flat ledge on gear.

Leave the ledge to the left onto 5.8 face that a tips-size crack protects, then continue left to the start of a big corner that faces right, and take it all the way to a huge ledge. Walk 20 ft right (the follower can be protected with a #2 or #4 first) to the obvious splitter and belay on 0.3 to 0.4 cams.

Climb the splitter finger crack, using knobs where helpful. When it pinches shut switch to the new crack on the left, then move right once the difficulties end and finish on easier ground to a belay ledge. Belay with a #3 cam.
Head toward the pitch 6 crack, visible from here, across third-class ground, with one brief fourth-class boulder problem toward the end. The belay is at the foot of the short crack.
Climb the crack above, starting on the right where it is unprotected. The route can be unroped here, with a five-minute scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches. No rappel table: the descent is by a different route with a single rappel mentioned.

pitch_detail.notes: A thin crack through the overhang to a ledge, then a hand crack leftward to a left-facing corner and the belay.
The corner goes up and over an overlap. The belay uses a bolt plus gear.
Climb face rightward and upward to a finger crack slanting left, which terminates on a ledge.
The dihedral runs to the broad ledge cutting across the whole formation.
Cracks up and right.
Traverse the face rightward below an overlap toward a tree; the cracks behind the tree (#0.5 to #1 cams) hold the crux. Ledges then lead to a corner facing right, with a tree belay at its top.
Work rightward over the face, then upward through a few plants.

The corner facing left leads to a leftward traverse into a layback crack, which turns into a straight-in crack; belay once past the overlap. Class 3 to low fifth class on the ridge then leads to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all eight pitches with lengths from feet.
review.other_findings: Stored grade is 5.11a/b; the hardest pitch the text grades is 5.11a.

pitch_detail.notes: A low-angle approach slab; the ice on it can be thin.
A stepped gully ending at a belay in an overhang right of the line. The steps are the physical difficulty, though reaching the belay can be the mental one.
A steep pillar attached to the rock that eases as you climb. Rappel from V-threads at the top, or continue up slabs above the ice.

review.changed: Wrote the three pitches; the open-ended upper slabs are left out. No rappel table: V-thread descent is mentioned only generally. Short screws are advised for the lower pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: The wide chimney in the large dihedral, ending at a belay atop the pillar (cams .4 to 1 take it). The rock is very solid though the chimney interior can feel glassy. The first 15 ft or so are unprotected unless you bring a #8 to bump inside; then a thin seam becomes a crack taking smaller gear, so carry very small gear if skipping the #8. Length is approximate.

Follow the crack straight up from the pillar top through a short overhang, traverse left under a small roof (exposed), then a different crack heads rightward over a bulge, and blocky cracks cross the final bulge to the top. Building a solid anchor in the talus above is difficult, and the route has no bolts. Length is approximate.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with the approximate lengths given.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.9+ is below the 5.10- the text gives for P2.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb to a sloping ledge just below the crux and stop there.
Pull the cruxes and exit onto a ramp, then go up and around until rope drag forces you to stop.
Up through a boulder-filled ledge to the left side of the wall beneath the main corner. Climb a 5.9 wide crack, then return to the base of the corner with big blocks.
Thread past large blocks to where the corner genuinely begins, then climb it to a small ledge that makes a fine stance.
Continue up the crack. Where the main system looks to get harder, step right around a corner for about 20 ft and back left into the main corner. The pitch ends at a ledge below the summit.
One 5.8 move gains the ramp below the summit. Traverse the ramp and go up easy ground on the left of the summit block.

rappel_detail.anchor: rope wrapped around the summit horn

rappel_detail.notes: Rapping the crack, the rope stuck three times. A better station here would help a lot; a backup anchor was built below to retrieve the rope.
Rap to the foot of the crack.
Rap to the ramp and downclimb to the next station.
Rap to the top of pitch 1.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches and six rappel stations as listed in the text; only R1 has a length. Climbing and rappelling used double 60 m ropes.

pitch_detail.notes: Cracks to a bolt-protected traverse, then more cracks.
Trend up and right.
Bolt-protected face on golden rock leading up and left to cracks, which take you to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches with lengths from feet. No rappel table: a single 70 m rope descent of the route is described, not stations.

pitch_detail.notes: Slab leading to a right-facing arching dihedral, with a couple of bolts.
An orange dihedral drifts leftward into a chimney; round it onto a spacious ledge.
Cracks in the face lead to a roof, which you pass. Further cracks veer left to another stance and anchor.
Cracks first drift right, then swing left, finishing at the top.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches with lengths from feet. No rappel table: a single 70 m rope descent is mentioned, not stations.

pitch_detail.notes: Blocks lead to a corner that is not deep. Clip four bolts there, then head up the steep arete prow. A few moves up and left bring you to an overhang, with three more bolts along the way. Stepping out right over the overhang is the crux; three further bolts lead to the anchor. Lower or rap from here (about 100 ft).
Three bolts lead to a second anchor, about 70 ft up. Descend by the third-class gully on the right.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with lengths from feet; no pitch grades given (5.12a is for the route). No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Grainy slab and fragile cobbles past five well-spaced bolts to a small ledge. Climb carefully.
Lower-angle slab past four widely spaced bolts to a crux bulge at the top, protected by three more closely spaced bolts. The rock is grainy and loose, so grades feel tough for the low angle.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; bolt count for P2 is four plus three as given. No rappel table: two rappels back to the base are mentioned only in general.
